chapter.title: Testing, accessibility and security
chapter.summary: A confidence-per-cost testing strategy with Testing Library, MSW and Playwright, accessibility from semantics to screen reader testing, and the browser attacks and defences every frontend engineer must know.

lessons.title: Frontend testing strategy and tools
lessons.summary: The testing trophy and confidence per cost, React Testing Library queries and user-event, MSW network mocking, Playwright E2E with auth reuse and traces, flaky tests, visual regression and CI layout.

parts.label: Strategy and RTL
parts.body:
## What tests are for

A test suite exists to let you **change code with confidence**. Every test buys some confidence and costs something: time to write, time to run, time to maintain when the implementation changes, and time lost to flakiness. A good frontend testing strategy maximises confidence per unit of cost. That framing, rather than a coverage number, is what interviewers want to hear.

Kent C. Dodds' guiding principle, which became the philosophy of Testing Library, is: **"The more your tests resemble the way your software is used, the more confidence they can give you."** A test that clicks a button labelled "Save" and checks that "Saved" appears survives refactors; a test that asserts a component's internal state variable changed breaks when you rename the variable and tells you nothing about whether users can save.

## The testing trophy

The classic test pyramid (many unit tests, fewer integration tests, very few end-to-end tests) came from backend systems where units are meaningful and UI tests were slow and brittle. Kent C. Dodds' **testing trophy** reshapes it for modern frontend work:

```text
            ___
           | E2E |            few: critical user journeys in a real browser
        ___|_____|___
       | Integration |        most: components with their children, real-ish data flow
       |_____________|
         |  Unit   |          some: pure logic, hooks, utilities
         |_________|
     ___________________
    |      Static       |     always: TypeScript, ESLint (including a11y rules)
    |___________________|
```

- **Static analysis** catches typos, type errors and many accessibility mistakes for almost no cost. TypeScript strict mode plus ESLint (with `jsx-a11y` and the React Hooks rules) is the base of the trophy.
- **Unit tests** suit pure logic: formatters, reducers, validation schemas, date maths, a pricing function. Fast and precise.
- **Integration tests** render a component (or a whole feature) with its real children, real state management and a mocked network, then interact with it like a user. This is where most frontend bugs are caught for the least cost, hence the trophy's widest band.
- **End-to-end (E2E) tests** run the real app in a real browser against a real or realistic backend. They give the most confidence and cost the most: slower, more moving parts, more flakiness. Reserve them for critical journeys: sign in, checkout, the core create-edit-delete flow.

The exact proportions matter less than the reasoning: **test at the level where a bug would be visible to the user, using the cheapest setup that still exercises real behaviour.**

## Component and integration tests with Testing Library

**React Testing Library** (RTL) renders components into a DOM (jsdom or happy-dom in Node, or a real browser with Vitest's browser mode) and gives you queries that find elements the way users and assistive technologies do.

### Query priority

Testing Library's docs ("About Queries") list a priority order. It doubles as an accessibility check: if you cannot find an element by role and name, a screen reader user may not be able to either.

| Priority | Query | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `getByRole` (with `name`) | `getByRole('button', { name: /save/i })` |
| 2 | `getByLabelText` | `getByLabelText('Email')` for form fields |
| 3 | `getByPlaceholderText` | Only when there is no label (which is itself a smell) |
| 4 | `getByText` | Non-interactive text content |
| 5 | `getByDisplayValue` | Current value of a filled form field |
| 6 | `getByAltText`, `getByTitle` | Images, titled elements |
| 7 | `getByTestId` | Last resort when nothing user-visible identifies the element |

### Query variants

| Variant | Not found | Found many | Async | Use for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `getBy...` | throws | throws | no | Element that should be there now |
| `queryBy...` | returns `null` | throws | no | Asserting something is **absent** |
| `findBy...` | rejects after timeout | rejects | yes (retries, default about 1 s) | Element that appears after async work |
| `getAllBy...` / `queryAllBy...` / `findAllBy...` | | returns array | | Lists |

### Interact like a user

Use `@testing-library/user-event` rather than `fireEvent`. `user.click()` produces the full sequence of pointer, mouse, focus and click events a browser would; `user.type()` fires key events character by character, respecting disabled and read-only fields. Call `userEvent.setup()` once per test and `await` each interaction.

### What a good integration test looks like

It renders the feature, mocks only the network boundary, performs the user's steps, and asserts on what the user would see. It does not reach into component state, does not mock child components, and does not assert on CSS class names.

### Common anti-patterns

- **Testing implementation details:** asserting on state, calling instance methods, checking that a specific hook was called, snapshotting the whole component tree. These break on refactors and miss real bugs.
- **Mocking your own components or hooks:** you end up testing the mocks. Mock at the boundaries: network, time, randomness, browser APIs that jsdom lacks.
- **Wrapping everything in `act()` manually:** RTL's `render`, `user-event` and `findBy` already handle it. An `act` warning usually means an async update finished after the test ended; await the UI change with `findBy` or `waitFor`.
- **`waitFor` with side effects inside**, or with many assertions: put one assertion inside and perform actions outside.
- **Snapshot tests of large components:** big diffs that reviewers approve without reading. Small, targeted inline snapshots of serialised data can be fine.

### jsdom's limits

jsdom implements the DOM but **not layout or rendering**: no real CSS cascade results for layout, `getBoundingClientRect()` returns zeros, no `IntersectionObserver` or `ResizeObserver` without polyfills, no real focus-visible behaviour, no scrolling. Tests that depend on visibility via CSS, layout, or real browser events belong in a real browser: Vitest browser mode (running component tests in Chromium, Firefox or WebKit via Playwright) or Playwright E2E.

## Unit tests and hooks

- Pure functions: plain Vitest (or Jest) tests with table-driven cases (`test.each`) covering edge cases: empty input, boundaries, invalid data, time zones.
- Custom hooks: prefer testing them through a small component that uses them; use `renderHook` when the hook is a reusable library unit.
- Time: fake timers (`vi.useFakeTimers()`) for debounce, polling and timeouts, and a fixed system time (`vi.setSystemTime`) for date logic. Remember to restore real timers, and note that fake timers can interfere with `user-event` unless configured with `advanceTimers`.

diagrams.title: Choosing the test level

parts.label: MSW, Playwright, visual
parts.body:
## Mocking the network with MSW

**Mock Service Worker (MSW)** intercepts requests at the network level instead of replacing `fetch` or your API client. In the browser it uses a real Service Worker; in Node (Vitest, Jest) it hooks into the request modules. Your application code runs unchanged: the same `fetch`, axios, GraphQL or React Query calls go out, and MSW answers them with handlers you define.

Why this is better than `vi.mock('./api')`:

- **Tests exercise the real data layer:** URL building, headers, serialisation, error handling, retries, caching in TanStack Query or SWR.
- **One set of handlers everywhere:** unit and integration tests, Storybook stories, local development without a backend, and Playwright runs if you want.
- **Failure cases are easy:** override a handler per test to return a 500, a 409, a slow response or malformed JSON.

MSW 2 uses the standard Fetch API classes:

```ts
import { http, HttpResponse, delay } from 'msw';

export const handlers = [
  http.get('/api/products/:id', ({ params }) =>
    HttpResponse.json({ id: params.id, name: 'Trail shoe', price: 129 }),
  ),
  http.get('/api/search', async ({ request }) => {
    const q = new URL(request.url).searchParams.get('q') ?? '';
    await delay(150); // realistic latency surfaces loading states
    return HttpResponse.json({ results: q ? [{ id: '1', title: `Result for ${q}` }] : [] });
  }),
];
```

Good practices:

- Set `onUnhandledRequest: 'error'` so a forgotten handler fails the test instead of silently hitting a real network.
- `server.resetHandlers()` after each test so per-test overrides do not leak.
- Keep handlers close to your API contract. Generating them or validating responses against an OpenAPI or zod schema prevents mocks drifting from the real API, the main weakness of any mocking approach.
- Do not mock what you do not own beyond the network: third-party SDKs often have their own test modes.

## End-to-end tests with Playwright

**Playwright** drives Chromium, Firefox and WebKit through one API. Its design removes the main sources of E2E flakiness that plagued older tools.

### Key concepts

- **Locators** are lazy descriptions of elements, re-resolved on every action: `page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Checkout' })`. They follow the same user-facing philosophy as Testing Library.
- **Auto-waiting:** before clicking, Playwright waits until the element is attached, visible, stable (not animating), enabled and receives events. No manual sleeps.
- **Web-first assertions** retry until they pass or time out: `await expect(page.getByRole('status')).toHaveText('Order placed')`. Never assert on a value read once (`expect(await locator.textContent()).toBe(...)`), which races the UI.
- **Isolation:** each test gets a fresh browser context (cookies, storage), cheap to create.
- **Fixtures** provide reusable setup (an authenticated page, seeded data) with automatic teardown.
- **Authentication once:** a setup project logs in and saves `storageState` to a file; tests reuse it instead of logging in through the UI every time.
- **Network control:** `page.route()` can stub or modify requests for edge cases, though for true E2E prefer a real backend with seeded data.
- **Debugging:** the **trace viewer** records a timeline of actions, DOM snapshots before and after each step, console logs and network requests. Configure `trace: 'on-first-retry'` in CI and open the trace for any failure.
- **Parallelism and sharding:** tests run in parallel workers, and `--shard=1/4` splits the suite across CI machines.

Playwright's "Best practices" page sums it up: test user-visible behaviour, keep tests isolated, avoid testing third-party sites you do not control, use locators and web-first assertions, and run across browsers in CI.

### What to cover with E2E

Pick the journeys whose failure would be an incident: sign-up or sign-in, search to product to cart to checkout, the main create and edit flow, permissions (a viewer cannot edit). Typically tens of tests, not thousands. Each should be independent, seed its own data through an API or database helper, and clean up.

### Flaky tests

A flaky test passes and fails without code changes. It erodes trust until people ignore red builds. Common causes and fixes:

| Cause | Fix |
|---|---|
| Fixed sleeps and racing assertions | Web-first assertions and `findBy`, never `waitForTimeout` |
| Shared state between tests (same user, same records) | Isolated data per test; unique ids; parallel-safe fixtures |
| Animations and transitions | Playwright waits for stability; disable animations in test mode (`prefers-reduced-motion` emulation or a CSS override) |
| Dependence on real time, time zones, locale | Fixed clock (`page.clock`), fixed `timezoneId` and `locale` in config |
| Third-party services | Stub them at the network layer |
| Order dependence | Run tests in random or parallel order to surface it |

Track flakiness explicitly: retries in CI (`retries: 2`) keep the pipeline moving, but a test that needed a retry should be reported and fixed, not hidden.

## Visual regression testing

Functional assertions do not notice that a button became invisible because of a CSS change, or that a layout broke at 375 px. **Visual regression tests** take screenshots and compare them with approved baselines.

- **Playwright:** `await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot('checkout.png', { mask: [page.getByTestId('timestamp')], maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.01 })`. The first run creates the baseline; later runs fail on differences beyond the threshold, and `--update-snapshots` accepts intentional changes. Baselines are per browser and platform, because font rendering differs, so generate and compare them in the same pinned environment (typically the official Playwright Docker image in CI).
- **Component-level:** Storybook stories captured by a service such as Chromatic or Percy, which handle baselines, review UI and cross-browser rendering. Every story becomes a visual test.
- **Stability rules:** mask dynamic content (dates, avatars, ads), freeze animations, use fixed data, wait for fonts and images to load, and keep screenshots focused (a component or region) rather than whole long pages, so diffs are reviewable.

Visual tests catch CSS regressions, design-system changes rippling across the app, and responsive breakages. Their cost is baseline maintenance and review time; reserve them for design-system components and key pages.

## Accessibility and contract checks in the pipeline

- Run **axe-core** in component tests (`vitest-axe` or `jest-axe`) and in Playwright (`@axe-core/playwright`) on key pages. Automated checks catch only part of accessibility issues, but they catch regressions cheaply.
- Playwright's **ARIA snapshots** (`toMatchAriaSnapshot`) assert on the accessibility tree structure of a region, which is both an a11y check and a robust structural assertion.
- **Contract tests** or schema validation between frontend and API (OpenAPI types, zod schemas shared with the server, or consumer-driven contracts) catch breaking API changes before E2E does.

## A CI pipeline that stays fast

```text
on every PR:
  typecheck + lint (incl. a11y lint)            ~1 min
  unit + integration tests (Vitest, MSW)        ~2-4 min, parallel
  build
  Playwright E2E smoke on Chromium (sharded)    ~5 min
  visual tests for changed components           async review
nightly or pre-release:
  full E2E across Chromium, Firefox, WebKit, mobile viewports
  full visual and axe sweep
```

Fast feedback keeps people running tests; the expensive, broad runs happen less often but still before release.

parts.label: Interview
parts.body:
## What interviewers are really testing

Testing questions reveal how you think about risk and cost. Interviewers listen for: a strategy grounded in confidence per cost (not a coverage target), tests that resemble user behaviour, mocking at boundaries, an understanding of what jsdom cannot do, how you keep E2E tests reliable, and how tests fit into CI. For senior roles: how you would introduce testing to a codebase with none, and how you handle flakiness at scale.

## Question 1: "How would you design the testing strategy for a new React app?"

**Model answer:**

> I think in terms of confidence per cost, roughly the testing trophy. The base is static analysis: TypeScript strict and ESLint with hooks and accessibility rules, because it is nearly free. Pure logic like pricing, validation and reducers gets fast unit tests. Most of the effort goes into integration tests with React Testing Library: render a feature with its real children and state, mock only the network with MSW, interact through user-event, and assert on what the user sees, queried by role and label. A small set of Playwright end-to-end tests covers the critical journeys like sign-in and checkout against a seeded backend, across browsers. Visual regression covers the design system and key pages. In CI, the fast layers run on every PR and the broad cross-browser runs nightly or before release. I track flaky tests as bugs.

## Question 2: "Why Testing Library's approach instead of testing component internals?"

**Model answer:** Tests that resemble usage survive refactors and catch what users would notice. If I assert on internal state or mock child components, renaming a variable breaks the test while a broken button might pass. Querying by role and accessible name also checks accessibility as a side effect: if `getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' })` fails, a screen reader user probably cannot find it either. Test ids are a last resort.

## Question 3: "getBy vs queryBy vs findBy?"

**Model answer:** `getBy` returns the element or throws, for things that should be there now. `queryBy` returns null instead of throwing, so it is the one for asserting absence. `findBy` returns a promise and retries until the element appears or a timeout passes, for UI that updates after async work. Using `getBy` right after an async action is the classic source of flaky tests; using `findBy` or a web-first assertion fixes it.

## Question 4: "How do you mock APIs in frontend tests?"

**Model answer:** At the network boundary with MSW rather than mocking my fetch wrapper or API module. The application's real data layer runs (URL building, headers, error handling, React Query caching), and MSW answers with handlers I can override per test for errors, slow responses or empty states. The same handlers power Storybook and local development. I set unhandled requests to error, reset handlers after each test, and keep handlers honest by typing or validating them against the API schema, because drifting mocks are the main risk.

## Question 5: "Your E2E suite is flaky. What do you do?"

**Model answer, structured:**

1. **Measure:** report tests that pass only on retry; rank by flake rate.
2. **Diagnose with traces:** Playwright trace viewer shows the DOM and network at each step of a failing run.
3. **Common fixes:** replace sleeps and one-shot reads with web-first assertions; give each test its own data; freeze time, locale and time zone; stub third-party services; disable animations; avoid order dependence.
4. **Process:** quarantine a flaky test with an owner and a deadline rather than letting it erode trust; keep retries for resilience but never as the fix.
5. **Rebalance:** if a scenario is flaky because it crosses too many systems, test most of it at the integration level and keep one E2E happy path.

## Question 6: "What can't you test in jsdom?"

**Model answer:** Anything that needs layout or real rendering: element sizes and positions, CSS-driven visibility, scrolling, intersection and resize observers without polyfills, real focus-visible behaviour, canvas drawing, and browser-specific quirks. For those I use Vitest's browser mode or Playwright component tests, which run in real Chromium, Firefox and WebKit, or cover them in E2E and visual tests.

## Question 7: "How do visual regression tests avoid being noisy?"

**Model answer:** Generate and compare screenshots in the same pinned environment, typically a Docker image, because fonts and anti-aliasing differ across operating systems. Mask dynamic regions like timestamps, use seeded data, disable animations, wait for fonts and images, and keep shots scoped to components or regions so diffs are reviewable. Use a small pixel threshold, and treat baseline updates as reviewed changes in the PR.

## Quick-fire follow-ups

| Follow-up | Strong short answer |
|---|---|
| "Why user-event over fireEvent?" | It simulates the full event sequence a real user produces, including focus and keyboard behaviour |
| "What is an act warning telling you?" | A state update happened outside a tracked interaction, usually async work finishing after the assertion; await the UI change |
| "Should you snapshot whole components?" | Rarely; big snapshots get rubber-stamped. Assert on behaviour instead |
| "Is 100% coverage a good goal?" | No; coverage shows what ran, not what was verified. Aim for confidence in critical paths |
| "How do you test auth flows in Playwright quickly?" | Log in once in a setup project, save `storageState`, reuse it |
| "Where do contract tests fit?" | Between frontend and API, catching breaking schema changes before E2E |

## Common mistakes

- Starting with a coverage target instead of a risk-based strategy.
- Mocking child components and internal modules, then testing the mocks.
- Using test ids everywhere instead of roles and labels.
- Fixed waits (`sleep`, `waitForTimeout`) in E2E tests.
- Shared accounts and data between parallel tests.
- Treating retries as the cure for flakiness.

keyPoints: Optimise for confidence per cost: static analysis, some unit tests, mostly integration tests, a few E2E tests for critical journeys.
Tests that resemble real usage survive refactors; query by role and accessible name, which also checks accessibility.
getBy for present elements, queryBy for asserting absence, findBy for elements that appear after async work; use user-event for interactions.
Mock at the network boundary with MSW so the real data layer runs; error on unhandled requests and keep handlers aligned with the API schema.
Playwright's locators, auto-waiting and web-first assertions remove most flakiness; reuse auth with storageState and debug failures with traces.
Visual regression needs a pinned rendering environment, masked dynamic content and scoped screenshots to stay reviewable.
jsdom has no layout; use Vitest browser mode or Playwright for layout, CSS visibility and real browser behaviour.

check.q: After clicking Save, a test immediately calls screen.getByText('Saved') and fails intermittently because the message appears after an API call. What is the right fix?
options: Add a 500 ms setTimeout before the assertion
Use getByTestId instead
Use await screen.findByText('Saved'), which retries until it appears or times out
Wrap the click in act() manually
check.why: findBy queries return a promise that retries until the element appears. Fixed sleeps are slow and still flaky, and act is already handled by RTL and user-event.

check.q: Why is mocking the network with MSW usually preferable to vi.mock on your API client module?
options: MSW makes tests run without a DOM
The application's real request code, error handling and caching still run, and the same handlers work in tests, Storybook and dev
MSW automatically generates assertions
vi.mock cannot mock modules that use fetch
check.why: Intercepting at the network level exercises URL building, headers, parsing and data-library behaviour, which module mocks replace. Handlers are reusable across environments.

check.q: Which practice best reduces flakiness in Playwright tests?
options: Web-first assertions such as await expect(locator).toHaveText(...) and isolated test data
Reading textContent once and comparing with toBe
Sharing one logged-in test account and its records across all parallel tests
Adding waitForTimeout(2000) after each navigation
check.why: Web-first assertions retry until the condition holds, matching asynchronous UI. Isolated data prevents parallel tests interfering. Fixed waits and one-shot reads race the UI.

lessons.title: Accessibility: WCAG, semantics, ARIA and keyboard
lessons.summary: The accessibility tree, WCAG 2.2 principles and key numbers, semantic HTML and the first rule of ARIA, keyboard and focus management, forms and live regions, accessible components and layered testing.

parts.label: WCAG, semantics, ARIA
parts.body:
## Why accessibility is an engineering topic

Accessibility (a11y) means people with disabilities can perceive, understand, navigate and interact with your product. That includes blind and low-vision users with screen readers or magnification, people who cannot use a mouse and rely on a keyboard, switch device or voice control, Deaf and hard-of-hearing users, people with cognitive or vestibular conditions, and everyone with a temporary or situational limitation (a broken arm, bright sunlight, a noisy train). The World Health Organization estimates about 1.3 billion people, roughly one in six, live with a significant disability.

It is also a legal requirement in many markets. The European Accessibility Act applies to many consumer-facing digital products and services in the EU from 28 June 2025, and laws such as the ADA in the US are routinely applied to websites. The common technical reference in these rules is **WCAG** at level AA.

For engineers the key insight is that **accessibility is mostly about using the platform correctly.** Native HTML elements come with keyboard support, focus behaviour and semantics that assistive technologies understand. Most accessibility bugs are introduced by rebuilding those elements from `div`s and forgetting what the browser gave you for free.

## How assistive technology sees your page

The browser builds an **accessibility tree** from the DOM and CSS, exposing each meaningful node with:

- a **role** (button, link, checkbox, heading level 2, navigation landmark, dialog),
- an **accessible name** ("Save draft"), computed from content, `aria-label`, `aria-labelledby`, an associated `label`, or `alt` text,
- an optional **description** (`aria-describedby`, such as a hint or error message),
- **states and properties** (checked, expanded, disabled, invalid, current page, selected).

Screen readers (NVDA and JAWS on Windows, VoiceOver on macOS and iOS, TalkBack on Android, Narrator) read this tree through operating-system accessibility APIs, and let users jump by headings, landmarks, links or form fields. If your tree is wrong, the experience is wrong, however good it looks. Chrome and Firefox DevTools both show the computed accessibility tree, role and name for any element.

## WCAG in one page

The **Web Content Accessibility Guidelines** are organised under four principles, **POUR**:

| Principle | Meaning | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Perceivable | Information is available to the senses users have | Text alternatives for images, captions, sufficient contrast, content that reflows at 400% zoom |
| Operable | Everything can be operated by the input users have | Full keyboard access, no keyboard traps, enough time, visible focus, no flashing content |
| Understandable | Content and behaviour are predictable | Labels and instructions, clear errors, consistent navigation, page language set |
| Robust | Works with current and future assistive technologies | Valid roles, names and states for all UI components |

Success criteria have levels **A** (minimum), **AA** (the usual legal and contractual target) and **AAA** (enhanced, not required as a whole). **WCAG 2.2** became a W3C Recommendation in October 2023. The W3C's "What's New in WCAG 2.2" page lists the additions, including:

- **2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), AA:** a focused element must not be entirely hidden by sticky headers, cookie banners or chat widgets.
- **2.5.7 Dragging Movements, AA:** anything done by dragging (reordering a list, a slider) must also be possible with single clicks or taps.
- **2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), AA:** pointer targets at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, or spaced so that a 24 px circle around each does not overlap others (with exceptions such as inline links).
- **3.2.6 Consistent Help, A** and **3.3.7 Redundant Entry, A:** help mechanisms in consistent places; do not make users re-enter information they already gave in the same process.
- **3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum), AA:** no cognitive function test (memorising, transcribing, solving puzzles) to log in unless there is an alternative; allowing paste and password managers usually satisfies it.

WCAG 2.2 also made 4.1.1 Parsing obsolete, since modern browsers parse HTML consistently.

Numbers worth memorising:

| Requirement | Value |
|---|---|
| Text contrast (AA) | 4.5:1 for normal text; 3:1 for large text (at least 18pt, or 14pt bold) |
| Non-text contrast (AA) | 3:1 for UI component boundaries, focus indicators, icons that convey meaning |
| Reflow (AA) | Usable at 320 CSS px width (400% zoom on a 1280 px screen) without two-dimensional scrolling |
| Text spacing (AA) | Content still works when users increase line height, paragraph, letter and word spacing |
| Target size (AA, 2.2) | 24 by 24 CSS px minimum (or adequate spacing) |
| Flashing (A) | No more than three flashes per second |

## Semantics first: use the right element

The most valuable rule is the **first rule of ARIA**: if a native HTML element or attribute has the semantics and behaviour you need, use it instead of adding ARIA to a generic element.

| Need | Use | Not |
|---|---|---|
| An action | `button` (type="button" outside forms) | `div` with a click handler |
| Navigation to a URL | `a` with `href` | `button` that sets `location`, or `a` without `href` |
| A form field label | `label` with `for` or wrapping the input | Placeholder text as the only label |
| Grouped options | `fieldset` with `legend` | A heading above unrelated inputs |
| A modal | `dialog` opened with `showModal()` | A `div` overlay with manual focus code |
| Page regions | `header`, `nav`, `main`, `aside`, `footer` (landmarks) | Generic `div`s |
| Structure | `h1` to `h6` in a logical outline | Bold text styled as headings |
| Disclosure | `details` and `summary` for simple cases | Custom toggles without state |
| Tabular data | `table` with `th` and `scope` | A grid of `div`s |

A `div` with `onClick` is not focusable, has no role, does not respond to Enter or Space, and is invisible to screen reader users as a control. Making it equivalent requires `role="button"`, `tabindex="0"`, key handlers for Enter and Space, and a disabled state, all of which a real `button` already has.

**Native `dialog` with `showModal()`** is now the right default for modals: it renders in the top layer, makes the rest of the page inert, moves focus into the dialog, closes on Escape, and returns focus to the opener in modern browsers. The `inert` attribute is also available directly to make background content non-interactive.

## ARIA: what it is and is not

**ARIA** (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) attributes change what the accessibility tree reports. They **do not add behaviour**: `role="button"` does not make an element focusable or keyboard operable. Use ARIA to:

1. **Name things** that have no visible text: `aria-label="Close"` on an icon button, or `aria-labelledby` pointing at visible text.
2. **Describe** with `aria-describedby`: hints, error messages, format requirements.
3. **Expose state:** `aria-expanded` on a disclosure button, `aria-pressed` on a toggle button, `aria-selected` on a tab, `aria-current="page"` on the active nav link, `aria-invalid` on a field with an error.
4. **Build composite widgets** that HTML lacks (tabs, combobox, tree, menu, grid), following the **ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG)** patterns for roles, states and keyboard interaction.
5. **Announce dynamic changes** with live regions (next part).

Common ARIA mistakes:

- `aria-label` on a non-interactive `div` or `span` (often ignored) instead of using visible text or a proper role.
- Contradicting native semantics: `button role="link"`, `h2 role="button"`.
- `aria-hidden="true"` on focusable content, creating focusable elements that screen readers cannot see.
- Using `role="menu"` for site navigation. Menus in ARIA are application menus with specific arrow-key behaviour; site navigation should be a `nav` with a list of links.
- Adding ARIA without the matching keyboard behaviour, which is worse than nothing because it promises a widget that does not work.

The APG puts it bluntly: "No ARIA is better than bad ARIA". WebAIM's annual analysis of the top million home pages has repeatedly found that pages using ARIA average more detected errors than pages without it. ARIA is powerful and easy to misuse.

diagrams.code:
flowchart LR
  DOM["DOM + CSS"] --> AT["Accessibility tree: role, name, description, states"]
  AT --> API["OS accessibility APIs"]
  API --> SR["Screen readers: NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, TalkBack"]
  API --> VC["Voice control and switch access"]
  N["Native button: role, name, focus, Enter and Space"] --> AT
  Dv["div with onClick: no role, not focusable"] -.->|"missing from AT as a control"| AT

parts.label: Keyboard, focus, forms
parts.body:
## Keyboard access

Many users never touch a mouse: screen reader users, people with motor impairments using keyboards or switch devices, power users. The rules:

1. **Everything interactive is reachable and operable by keyboard.** Tab and Shift+Tab move between controls; Enter activates links and buttons; Space activates buttons and toggles checkboxes; arrow keys move within composite widgets (radio groups, tabs, menus, listboxes, grids); Escape closes dialogs and popups.
2. **Focus order follows visual and logical order.** It comes from DOM order. Do not fix it with positive `tabindex` values (`tabindex="3"`), which create an order separate from the DOM and are almost always wrong. Fix the DOM order, and be careful with CSS that visually reorders (`order`, `flex-direction: row-reverse`, grid placement).
3. **No keyboard traps.** Users must be able to leave every component with standard keys. The exception is a modal dialog, which should contain focus while open, and Escape closes it.
4. **Focus is always visible.** Never remove outlines without replacing them. Use `:focus-visible` to show a strong indicator for keyboard users without showing it on mouse click, with at least 3:1 contrast against adjacent colours. WCAG 2.2 also requires that the focused element is not fully hidden behind sticky headers or banners (`scroll-padding-top` helps).
5. **Skip links:** a "Skip to main content" link as the first focusable element lets keyboard users bypass repeated navigation.

### `tabindex` values

| Value | Effect | Use |
|---|---|---|
| none (native control) | Focusable in DOM order | Default: use native elements |
| `0` | Adds a non-native element to the tab order in DOM order | Custom widgets that must be focusable |
| `-1` | Focusable by script (`el.focus()`), not by Tab | Headings or containers you move focus to programmatically; inactive items in roving tabindex |
| positive | Jumps ahead of DOM order | Avoid |

### Composite widgets: one tab stop

For widgets like tabs, toolbars, radio groups, menus and grids, the APG pattern is **one tab stop for the whole widget**, with arrow keys moving between items. Two techniques:

- **Roving tabindex:** the active item has `tabindex="0"`, all others `tabindex="-1"`. Arrow keys move the `0` and call `focus()` on the new item. Simple and robust.
- **`aria-activedescendant`:** focus stays on a container (or a combobox input), and `aria-activedescendant` points to the id of the visually highlighted option. Used for comboboxes and listboxes where focus must stay in a text input.

## Focus management in single-page apps

Browsers handle focus on full page loads: a new page starts at the top, and screen readers announce the new title. Client-side routing breaks this: the URL and content change, but focus stays on the link the user clicked (which may no longer exist), and nothing is announced. Fixes:

- **On route change, move focus** to the main heading (`h1` with `tabindex="-1"`) or the main region, and update `document.title`. Some routers announce route changes with a live region; Next.js includes a route announcer that reads the new page title.
- **Opening a dialog** moves focus into it (to the first focusable element, or the dialog heading). **Closing** returns focus to the element that opened it. Native `dialog` with `showModal()` handles most of this.
- **Deleting an item** moves focus to a sensible neighbour (the next item, or the list heading), never to `body`.
- **Showing inline errors** after submit moves focus to the first invalid field or to an error summary at the top of the form.

## Forms

Forms are where accessibility failures cost conversions directly.

- Every field has a visible, programmatically associated **label**. Placeholders disappear on typing and have poor contrast; they are hints, not labels.
- Group related controls (radio buttons, address parts) with `fieldset` and `legend`.
- Mark required fields in text and with `required` (or `aria-required`), not only with colour or an asterisk without explanation.
- Use the right `type` and `autocomplete` values (`email`, `tel`, `autocomplete="current-password"`, `one-time-code`) so browsers, password managers and mobile keyboards help, which also supports WCAG's accessible authentication and redundant entry criteria.
- **Errors:** describe what went wrong and how to fix it in text, associate the message with the field via `aria-describedby`, set `aria-invalid="true"`, and on submit either focus the first invalid field or show an error summary with links to each field. Do not rely on colour alone.
- Do not disable the submit button until the form is valid without explanation; users cannot tell what is missing. Validate on submit (and on blur for specific fields) and explain.

## Dynamic content and live regions

When content changes without a page load (a toast, a search result count, a "saved" message, a chat message), sighted users notice; screen reader users do not, unless you announce it.

- `role="status"` (implicit `aria-live="polite"`) announces when the user is idle: "12 results", "Draft saved".
- `role="alert"` (implicit `aria-live="assertive"`) interrupts: errors that need immediate attention. Use sparingly.
- The live region element must **exist in the DOM before** its content changes. Inserting a new element that already contains text is announced unreliably; render an empty region on mount and update its text.
- Keep announcements short, avoid announcing every keystroke (debounce result counts), and do not put whole widgets inside live regions.
- Loading states: `aria-busy="true"` on a region being updated, plus a polite status message such as "Loading results".

## Visual design concerns engineers own

- **Colour contrast** per the WCAG numbers; check design tokens once and the whole design system benefits. Include states: hover, disabled (exempt, but should still be distinguishable), focus rings, placeholder text, text on images.
- **Never use colour alone** to convey meaning: add icons, text or patterns to error states, chart series and status badges.
- **Respect user preferences:** `prefers-reduced-motion` (disable parallax and large animations, which can trigger vestibular disorders), `prefers-color-scheme`, `forced-colors` (Windows High Contrast: do not rely on background images or box shadows for essential information).
- **Zoom and reflow:** use relative units, avoid fixed heights that clip text, do not disable pinch zoom (`user-scalable=no`), and test at 200% and 400% zoom and at 320 px width.
- **Images:** informative images need `alt` that conveys the purpose; decorative images get `alt=""` so they are skipped; complex images (charts) need a text alternative or data table nearby. Icon-only buttons need an accessible name.
- **Media:** captions for video, transcripts for audio, no autoplaying sound, and pause controls for anything moving for more than five seconds.

## Building accessible components

For any custom component, follow the matching APG pattern and verify four things: correct role, accessible name, states exposed and updated, and complete keyboard interaction. Better still, build on well-tested headless libraries (React Aria, Radix UI, Ark UI, Headless UI) that implement APG patterns, and style them yourself. Writing an accessible combobox or date picker from scratch is a multi-week project that most teams get wrong.

sequenceDiagram

  participant B as Open button
  participant D as dialog (showModal)
  participant P as Page behind
  U->>B: Enter
  B->>D: showModal()
  D->>P: rest of page becomes inert

  U->>D: Escape
  D->>B: close, focus returns to opener

parts.label: Testing and interview
parts.body:
## Testing accessibility

No single method finds everything. A layered approach, cheapest first:

**1. Linting while you type.** `eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y` flags missing `alt`, click handlers on non-interactive elements, invalid ARIA attributes, and labels without controls. Free and immediate.

**2. Automated checks in tests and CI.** **axe-core** (by Deque) evaluates rendered pages against a large set of WCAG rules: contrast, missing names, invalid ARIA, duplicate ids, landmark problems.

- In component tests: `vitest-axe` or `jest-axe` on rendered components. Note that jsdom cannot compute colour contrast reliably, so run contrast checks in a real browser.
- In Playwright: `@axe-core/playwright` scans whole pages or specific regions after interactions (open the menu, then scan). Playwright's "Accessibility testing" guide shows the setup.
- Playwright's ARIA snapshots (`toMatchAriaSnapshot`) assert on the accessibility tree of a region, catching regressions in roles and names.

Automated tools find a meaningful share of issues, but far from all: Deque's own research estimates axe finds around 57% of issues by volume. They cannot judge whether alt text is meaningful, whether focus order makes sense, whether an error message is understandable, or whether a custom widget is usable with a screen reader.

**3. Manual keyboard testing.** Unplug the mouse and use the feature: Tab through everything, check visible focus at each step, operate every control with Enter, Space, arrows and Escape, make sure you never get stuck, and check that focus moves sensibly when dialogs open and close or content is deleted. This takes minutes per feature and catches the most impactful bugs.

**4. Screen reader testing.** Test the main flows with at least one combination: VoiceOver with Safari on macOS and iOS, NVDA with Firefox or Chrome on Windows, TalkBack with Chrome on Android. Check that headings and landmarks give a usable outline, controls announce role, name and state, and dynamic updates are announced.

**5. Zoom, reflow and preferences.** 200% and 400% zoom, 320 px width, increased text spacing, Windows forced colours, reduced motion.

**6. Users with disabilities.** Nothing replaces usability testing with real assistive technology users, ideally for core flows before major launches.

### Accessibility in the development process

- Bake it into the **design system**: accessible primitives (button, dialog, menu, combobox, tooltip), contrast-checked tokens, focus styles. Fixing a component fixes every usage.
- Add a11y acceptance criteria to tickets ("keyboard operable, announced on save").
- Run axe on key pages in CI and fail on new serious or critical violations.
- Include a keyboard pass in code review for UI changes.
- Track and fix issues like any other bug, prioritised by user impact.

## What interviewers are really testing

Accessibility questions show whether you build UI for everyone or only for yourself. Interviewers look for: semantic HTML as the default, a correct mental model of ARIA (names and states, no behaviour), keyboard and focus management, the WCAG basics with real numbers, and a realistic testing approach that goes beyond running Lighthouse. Senior frontend roles increasingly include "build an accessible component" exercises (modal, tabs, combobox, dropdown).

## Question 1: "How do you make a custom dropdown or modal accessible?"

**Model answer (modal):**

> I start with the native `dialog` element opened with `showModal()`, which gives me the top layer, an inert background, Escape to close and focus moved inside. I give it an accessible name with `aria-labelledby` pointing at its heading, make sure the first focus goes somewhere sensible, and return focus to the button that opened it on close. Tab stays within the dialog. If I cannot use the native element, I implement the APG dialog pattern: `role="dialog"` with `aria-modal`, a focus trap, `inert` on the rest of the page, Escape handling and focus restoration. Then I test with a keyboard and a screen reader, not just axe.

For a select-like dropdown, the first question is whether a native `select` works. If it must be custom, it is the APG listbox or combobox pattern: a button or input with `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls`, options with `role="option"` and `aria-selected`, arrow keys, Home and End, type-ahead, Escape, and `aria-activedescendant` or roving focus. Or use a tested headless library.

## Question 2: "What is the first rule of ARIA?"

**Model answer:** Do not use ARIA if a native HTML element or attribute gives you the semantics and behaviour you need. ARIA only changes what assistive technology is told; it adds no keyboard support or focusability. A `div` with `role="button"` still needs `tabindex`, Enter and Space handling and disabled logic, while a `button` has it all. Bad ARIA is worse than none because it promises behaviour that is not there.

## Question 3: "How do you handle focus in a single-page app on route change?"

**Model answer:** Client-side navigation does not reset focus or announce the new page. After a route change, I update the document title and move focus to the main heading, which has `tabindex="-1"`, or announce the new page through a live region, as Next.js's route announcer does. For in-page changes: dialogs receive focus and return it on close, deleted items move focus to a neighbour, and failed form submissions focus the first invalid field or an error summary.

## Question 4: "Which WCAG numbers should a frontend engineer know?"

**Model answer:** AA contrast of 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text and for UI components and focus indicators. Content reflows at 320 CSS pixels wide (400% zoom) without horizontal scrolling. Target size of at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels under WCAG 2.2. No more than three flashes per second. And the 2.2 additions: focus not obscured by sticky elements, single-pointer alternatives to dragging, and accessible authentication that allows paste and password managers.

## Question 5: "How do you test accessibility in a large app?"

**Model answer:** Layers: ESLint a11y rules in the editor; axe in component tests and in Playwright on key pages after interactions, failing CI on new serious violations; ARIA snapshots for critical regions. But automated tools catch only part of the problems, so every UI change gets a quick keyboard pass, and main flows are checked with a screen reader regularly. Most leverage comes from making the design-system primitives accessible, and for major launches, testing with disabled users.

## Question 6: "When would you use aria-live, and what are the pitfalls?"

**Model answer:** For changes that happen without focus moving, like "saved", result counts or validation summaries. `role="status"` is polite and waits; `role="alert"` interrupts and is for urgent errors only. The region must already exist in the DOM before its text changes, announcements should be short, and frequent updates should be debounced so the screen reader is not flooded.

## Quick-fire follow-ups

| Follow-up | Strong short answer |
|---|---|
| "alt text for a decorative image?" | `alt=""` so screen readers skip it |
| "Positive tabindex?" | Avoid; fix DOM order instead |
| "`aria-hidden` on a focusable element?" | A bug: focusable but invisible to screen readers |
| "Placeholder as label?" | No; it disappears and has low contrast. Use a real label |
| "`:focus` vs `:focus-visible`?" | `:focus-visible` shows the indicator when the browser judges it useful, typically keyboard use |
| "How to hide visually but keep for screen readers?" | A visually-hidden (sr-only) CSS class, not `display: none` |
| "Does Lighthouse 100 mean accessible?" | No; it runs a subset of automated checks |

## Common mistakes

- Rebuilding buttons, links and selects from `div`s.
- Treating ARIA roles as if they add keyboard behaviour.
- Removing focus outlines for aesthetics without a replacement.
- Relying on colour alone for errors, status or chart series.
- Live regions inserted together with their content, so nothing is announced.
- Declaring a feature accessible because axe or Lighthouse found nothing.

keyPoints: Assistive technologies read the accessibility tree: role, accessible name, description and states derived from DOM, CSS and ARIA.

WCAG is organised as Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust; AA is the usual legal target, and WCAG 2.2 added focus not obscured, dragging alternatives, target size and accessible authentication.
Use native elements first; ARIA only changes what is announced and adds no behaviour, and bad ARIA is worse than none.
Everything must work by keyboard with visible focus and logical DOM order; composite widgets use one tab stop with roving tabindex or aria-activedescendant.
SPAs must manage focus on route changes, dialogs, deletions and form errors; native dialog with showModal handles most modal behaviour.
Live regions must exist before their content changes; use status for polite updates and alert only for urgent errors.
Test in layers: lint, axe in component and Playwright tests, manual keyboard passes, screen readers, zoom and real users; automated tools catch only part.

check.q: A developer adds role="button" to a div with an onClick handler. What is still missing for keyboard users?
options: Nothing; the role makes it fully equivalent to a button
Only an aria-label
Only a CSS cursor: pointer
Focusability (tabindex="0") and Enter and Space key handling, which a native button provides automatically
check.why: ARIA roles change what assistive technology is told but add no behaviour. A native button is focusable and activates on Enter and Space; the div needs all of that added manually.

check.q: After a client-side route change in a React SPA, a screen reader user hears nothing and focus stays on the clicked link. What is a correct fix?
options: Update document.title and move focus to the new page's main heading (tabindex="-1") or announce the change via a live region
Add tabindex="1" to the main content
Reload the page on every navigation
Set aria-hidden on the navigation
check.why: Full page loads reset focus and announce the title; client-side routing does not. Moving focus to the heading or announcing the new page restores that context.

check.q: Which statement about automated accessibility testing with axe is accurate?
options: A clean axe run proves WCAG AA conformance
axe can judge whether alt text is meaningful
It catches many issues cheaply, such as missing names and invalid ARIA, but cannot verify focus order logic, meaningful text or real screen reader usability
axe replaces the need for keyboard testing
check.why: Automated rules cover a portion of issues. Judgement-based criteria and actual usability with assistive technology need manual keyboard and screen reader testing.

lessons.title: Frontend security: XSS, CSP, CSRF, CORS and supply chain
lessons.summary: XSS types, sources and sinks and where frameworks stop protecting you, strict CSP and Trusted Types, token storage, CSRF and SameSite, what CORS really does, clickjacking, and supply-chain defences.

parts.label: XSS, CSP, Trusted Types
parts.body:
## The frontend threat model

The browser runs code from many sources in one page: your bundle, third-party scripts, data from your API that originally came from other users, and browser extensions. The browser's **same-origin policy** (scheme + host + port) is the main wall: a script from one origin cannot read data from another. Most frontend attacks are about getting around that wall: running the attacker's script **inside** your origin (XSS), making the victim's browser send **authenticated requests** they did not intend (CSRF), tricking them into **clicking** something on your page (clickjacking), or compromising the **code you ship** (supply chain).

OWASP's cheat sheets are the best concise references for each; this lesson leans on them heavily.

## Cross-site scripting (XSS)

XSS happens when attacker-controlled data is interpreted as code in your page. Once a script runs in your origin it can do anything the user can: read the DOM (including CSRF tokens and personal data), call your APIs with the user's cookies, change the page to phish for passwords, or log keystrokes. It does **not** need to read an `HttpOnly` cookie to cause damage; it can simply make requests as the user.

| Type | Where the payload lives | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Stored | Your database | A comment containing a script tag rendered to every viewer |
| Reflected | The request (URL, form) echoed in the response | A search page that prints `q` unescaped |
| DOM-based | Client-side code moves data from a source to a sink | `el.innerHTML = location.hash.slice(1)` |

**Sources** are attacker-influenced inputs: URL parts, `postMessage` data, `localStorage`, API responses containing user content. **Sinks** are APIs that interpret strings as HTML or code: `innerHTML`, `outerHTML`, `insertAdjacentHTML`, `document.write`, `eval`, `new Function`, `setTimeout` with a string, `javascript:` URLs in `href` or `src`, and some attributes like `srcdoc`.

### What frameworks give you, and where they stop

React, Vue, Angular and Svelte **escape text by default**: `{comment.body}` in JSX becomes a text node, so a script tag shows up as literal text. That kills most classic XSS. The remaining holes are explicit or subtle:

1. **`dangerouslySetInnerHTML`** (and `v-html`, `[innerHTML]`, `{@html}`): you are now responsible. Sanitise with a maintained sanitiser such as **DOMPurify** right before insertion, with a strict allow-list, or better, avoid HTML entirely by rendering Markdown to React elements with a library that does not allow raw HTML.
2. **URLs in attributes:** `<a href={user.website}>` with `javascript:alert(1)` executes on click. React warns about `javascript:` URLs, but you should validate that user-supplied URLs use `http:` or `https:` (parse with `new URL()` and check `protocol`).
3. **Direct DOM access** in effects or refs: `ref.current.innerHTML = ...` bypasses React's escaping.
4. **Server-rendered HTML outside the framework:** templates, emails, or JSON embedded in a script tag for hydration. Serialising state into a script tag without escaping `<` lets `</script>` in data break out. Use the framework's serialiser.
5. **Third-party widgets** that use `innerHTML` with data you pass them.
6. **Rendering LLM output:** treat model output as untrusted user input; never inject it as HTML without sanitising.

The OWASP XSS Prevention Cheat Sheet's core rule: **encode output for the context it lands in** (HTML body, attribute, URL, JavaScript, CSS), and prefer safe APIs (`textContent`, `setAttribute` for non-URL attributes, framework bindings) over string-built HTML.

## Content Security Policy (CSP)

CSP is a response header that tells the browser which scripts and other resources the page may load and execute. It is **defence in depth**: if an injection slips through, a strict CSP stops the injected script from running.

Old-style allow-list policies (`script-src 'self' cdn.example.com analytics.example.com`) are weak: any JSONP endpoint, old library or user-upload path on an allowed host can be abused, and research by Google found most allow-list policies bypassable. web.dev's "Mitigate XSS with a strict CSP" recommends a **strict CSP** based on nonces or hashes:

```text
Content-Security-Policy:
  script-src 'nonce-R4nd0mPerRequest' 'strict-dynamic' https: 'unsafe-inline';
  object-src 'none';
  base-uri 'none';
  frame-ancestors 'self';
  report-to csp-endpoint
```

How it works:

- The server generates a fresh random **nonce** per response and adds it to every legitimate script tag (`nonce="R4nd0mPerRequest"`). Injected scripts do not know the nonce and are blocked.
- **`'strict-dynamic'`** lets scripts that were trusted via the nonce load further scripts (bundler chunks, tag managers), so you do not need to list hosts.
- `https:` and `'unsafe-inline'` are **fallbacks for old browsers**; browsers that understand nonces and `strict-dynamic` ignore them.
- `object-src 'none'` blocks plugin content; `base-uri 'none'` stops an injected `base` tag from redirecting relative script URLs.
- Inline event handlers (`onclick="..."`) and `javascript:` URLs are blocked, which is good and also means you must not rely on them.
- **Static sites** that cannot generate per-request nonces use **hashes** of inline scripts instead (`'sha256-...'`).

Rollout: start with **`Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only`** and a reporting endpoint (`Reporting-Endpoints` header plus `report-to`), fix the violations your own code causes, then enforce. Frameworks help: Next.js can generate nonces in `proxy.ts` and apply them to its scripts, at the cost of making those pages dynamically rendered.

## Trusted Types

CSP stops injected script tags, but DOM-based XSS through sinks like `innerHTML` can still happen within your own trusted code. **Trusted Types** close that gap. With the CSP directive `require-trusted-types-for 'script'`, the browser **refuses plain strings** at dangerous sinks: `el.innerHTML = str` throws unless `str` is a `TrustedHTML` object created by a policy you defined.

```ts
const policy = trustedTypes.createPolicy('sanitize', {
  createHTML: (input) => DOMPurify.sanitize(input), // the only way to make TrustedHTML
});
el.innerHTML = policy.createHTML(userHtml);
```

The benefit is architectural: instead of auditing every `innerHTML` in the codebase and every dependency, you audit the few policies. web.dev's "Prevent DOM-based XSS with Trusted Types" describes how Google applied it widely. Pair it with `trusted-types <policy names>` to restrict which policies may be created. Chromium has supported Trusted Types since 2020 and other engines have been adding it; check current compatibility data. Roll out in report-only mode first, because dependencies that use `innerHTML` will show up as violations.

## Storing tokens in the browser

Where you keep credentials changes what XSS can do:

| Storage | Readable by injected JS? | Sent automatically? | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite` cookie | No | Yes, to its site | Needs CSRF protection; XSS can still make requests as the user but cannot steal the token for later use |
| `localStorage` / `sessionStorage` | Yes | No | Any XSS can exfiltrate long-lived tokens |
| In-memory variable | Yes, while page is open | No | Lost on reload; often paired with a refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie |

For most web apps, an `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Lax` (or `Strict`) session cookie with a `__Host-` prefix is the safest default. It does not make XSS harmless, but it limits damage to the session's lifetime and to actions the attacker can perform while the user's page is open.

parts.label: CSRF, CORS, clickjacking
parts.body:
## Cross-site request forgery (CSRF)

CSRF abuses the fact that browsers attach cookies automatically. If `bank.example` authenticates with a cookie, a page on `evil.example` can submit a hidden form to `https://bank.example/transfer`, and the browser sends the victim's cookie along. The attacker cannot read the response (the same-origin policy prevents that), but the state-changing request already happened.

```text
victim logged in to bank.example (session cookie)
visits evil.example
  evil page auto-submits <form action="https://bank.example/transfer" method="POST">
  browser attaches bank.example cookies (if SameSite allows)
  bank sees a valid session -> performs the transfer
```

### Defences, layered

1. **SameSite cookies.** `SameSite=Lax` means the cookie is not sent on cross-site subrequests (forms POSTed from another site, `fetch`, images, iframes) but is sent on top-level GET navigations (clicking a link to your site). `SameSite=Strict` never sends it cross-site, which also logs users out when they arrive from an external link. Chromium treats cookies without a `SameSite` attribute as `Lax` by default, but not every browser does, so **set it explicitly**. Two limits: Lax still allows cross-site top-level GETs, so **never change state on GET**; and SameSite is about *sites* (registrable domain), so a compromised or user-controlled subdomain (`user-content.example.com`) counts as same-site.
2. **Check `Origin` (and Fetch Metadata) on state-changing requests.** Browsers send `Origin` on cross-origin POSTs and on most same-origin ones, and `Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin | same-site | cross-site | none` on all requests in modern browsers. Rejecting non-safe methods where `Sec-Fetch-Site` is `cross-site` (or `Origin` is not yours) is a simple, robust server-side check. Next.js applies an Origin-vs-Host check to Server Actions for this reason.
3. **CSRF tokens** for cookie-authenticated forms, especially if you must support older browsers or same-site attackers: the synchroniser token pattern (a random token tied to the session, embedded in the form and verified server-side) or a signed double-submit cookie. The OWASP CSRF Prevention Cheat Sheet details both, and recommends signing double-submit tokens to the session rather than the naive version.
4. **Require a custom header or JSON content type** for API calls. Cross-site forms cannot set custom headers, and a cross-origin `fetch` with them triggers a CORS preflight that your server will refuse. Helpful, but do not rely on it alone.

APIs authenticated with an `Authorization: Bearer` header instead of cookies are not vulnerable to classic CSRF, because the browser does not attach that header automatically. They are, however, exposed to token theft by XSS if the token is readable by JavaScript.

## CORS: what it is and what it is not

The same-origin policy stops a script on `app.example` from **reading** responses from `api.other.com`. **CORS** (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is how a server **relaxes** that rule for specific origins. The key misconception to correct in interviews: **CORS is not a security feature that protects your server.** It protects users' data in *other* origins from being read by your page, and it is enforced by the browser only. Curl, servers and attackers' scripts outside a browser ignore it entirely.

How it works:

- **Simple requests** (GET, HEAD or POST with only simple headers and content types `text/plain`, `multipart/form-data` or `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`) are sent directly. The browser then checks the response's `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` before letting your script read it. Note the request **was sent and processed** regardless, which is why CORS does not stop CSRF.
- **Preflighted requests** (PUT, DELETE, PATCH, a JSON content type, custom headers like `Authorization`) first send an `OPTIONS` request with `Access-Control-Request-Method` and `Access-Control-Request-Headers`. Only if the server answers with matching `Access-Control-Allow-*` headers does the browser send the real request. `Access-Control-Max-Age` caches the preflight.
- **Credentials:** to include cookies, the client sets `credentials: 'include'` and the server must respond with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` **and a specific origin**, never `*`.

Common CORS vulnerabilities, all server-side misconfigurations:

| Misconfiguration | Risk |
|---|---|
| Reflecting any `Origin` back with `Allow-Credentials: true` | Any site can read authenticated responses: data theft |
| Allowing the `null` origin | Sandboxed iframes and some redirects send `null`; attackers can use them |
| Prefix or suffix matching (`endsWith('example.com')`) | `evilexample.com` passes |
| Trusting all subdomains | One XSS on any subdomain reads your API |
| Missing `Vary: Origin` with dynamic allow-origin | Caches serve one origin's CORS headers to another |

The MDN CORS guide is the clearest reference on the exact rules.

## Clickjacking

An attacker loads your page in an invisible iframe on their site and positions it under a decoy button ("Claim your prize"). The victim's click lands on your real "Delete account" or "Authorise" button, with their real session.

Defence: tell the browser who may frame you.

- **`Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'`** (no framing) or `'self'` (only your own pages), or a list of trusted origins. This is the modern control.
- **`X-Frame-Options: DENY`** or `SAMEORIGIN` for older browsers. It cannot express multiple allowed origins.
- For sensitive one-click actions, require re-confirmation (re-enter password, a second step) so a single hijacked click is not enough.

JavaScript "frame-busting" scripts are unreliable; use headers. The OWASP Clickjacking Defense Cheat Sheet covers edge cases.

## Other browser-side issues worth knowing

- **`postMessage`:** always check `event.origin` against an allow-list before trusting a message, and pass a specific `targetOrigin` (not `'*'`) when sending sensitive data.
- **Reverse tabnabbing:** a page opened with `target="_blank"` could navigate its opener via `window.opener`. Modern browsers now imply `rel="noopener"` for `target="_blank"` links, but set it explicitly for `window.open` and older browser support.
- **Open redirects:** `/login?next=https://evil.example` used after login turns your domain into a phishing tool. Only allow relative paths or an allow-list of hosts.
- **Prototype pollution:** merging untrusted JSON into objects (`__proto__` keys) can change behaviour across the app, sometimes turning into XSS through gadget code. Use `Object.create(null)`, `Map`, or libraries that guard against it, and validate input shapes with schemas.
- **Sensitive data in the client:** anything in your bundle, RSC payload, `localStorage` or source maps is public. API keys for paid services, internal URLs and feature flags for unreleased features do not belong there.
- **Security headers baseline:** `Strict-Transport-Security` (HSTS), `Content-Security-Policy`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin`, `Permissions-Policy` to disable unused powerful features, and cross-origin isolation headers (`Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy`) where needed.
