sequenceDiagram
  participant P as Page on app.example
  participant B as Browser
  participant A as api.other.com
  P->>B: fetch PUT /items with JSON and credentials
  B->>A: OPTIONS preflight (Origin, Access-Control-Request-Method PUT)
  A-->>B: Allow-Origin app.example, Allow-Methods PUT, Allow-Credentials true
  B->>A: PUT /items with cookies
  A-->>B: 200 JSON with Allow-Origin app.example
  B-->>P: response readable by script
  Note over B,A: Without matching headers the browser blocks the read, not the server

parts.label: Supply chain, interview
parts.body:
## Supply chain: the code you did not write

A typical frontend app ships code from hundreds of npm packages and loads a handful of third-party scripts at runtime. Each is code running with your origin's privileges. Supply-chain attacks target that trust instead of your code, and they have become one of the most common ways frontends are compromised.

Real incidents worth knowing (and naming in interviews):

- **event-stream (2018):** a popular package was handed to a new "maintainer" who added a dependency with code targeting a specific Bitcoin wallet app.
- **ua-parser-js (2021):** a maintainer's npm account was hijacked and malicious versions installing crypto miners and password stealers were published.
- **polyfill.io (2024):** the domain behind a widely embedded polyfill CDN changed hands, and the service began injecting malicious redirects into the script served to many thousands of sites. Every site that loaded it from a third-party URL was affected without deploying anything.
- **September 2025 npm compromises:** a maintainer of very widely used packages (such as `chalk` and `debug`) was phished, and malicious versions that tried to hijack crypto transactions in browsers were briefly published. Days later the self-replicating **Shai-Hulud** worm spread through stolen npm tokens, publishing infected versions of hundreds of packages.

The pattern: attackers compromise a maintainer account, a domain, or a build pipeline, and every downstream consumer installs or loads the malicious code automatically.

### Defences for dependencies

| Control | What it prevents |
|---|---|
| Commit the lockfile; install with `npm ci` (or `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`) in CI | Silent upgrades to a newly published malicious version |
| Review dependency diffs in PRs; prefer fewer, well-maintained dependencies | Dragging in abandoned or single-maintainer packages for trivial functions |
| Automated updates (Renovate, Dependabot) with a delay or minimum release age | Installing a malicious version in the hours before it is detected and unpublished |
| Disable install scripts by default (`ignore-scripts`, or package managers that only run allow-listed build scripts) | Malware that runs on `npm install` in developer machines and CI |
| `npm audit`, GitHub advisories, Socket or Snyk scanning | Known-vulnerable or known-malicious versions |
| Provenance attestations and npm trusted publishing (OIDC from CI, no long-lived tokens) for packages you publish | Your own packages being published from a stolen token |
| Least-privilege CI secrets; separate build and deploy credentials | A compromised dev dependency exfiltrating production secrets from CI |

### Defences for third-party scripts at runtime

- **Self-host** third-party libraries where licences allow, so a change at someone else's CDN does not change your site.
- When loading from a CDN, use **Subresource Integrity**: an `integrity="sha384-..."` attribute (plus `crossorigin="anonymous"`) makes the browser refuse the file if its hash changes. SRI only works for static, versioned files; services that generate per-browser responses (as polyfill.io did) cannot be pinned, which is itself a reason to avoid them.
- A **strict CSP** limits what injected or compromised scripts can load or where they can send data (`connect-src`), and violation reports alert you to changes.
- **Sandbox** untrusted widgets in cross-origin iframes with the `sandbox` attribute, communicating via `postMessage` with origin checks.
- Keep an **inventory** of every tag in your tag manager with an owner, because marketing tags added without a deploy run with the same privileges as your code.

## What interviewers are really testing

Frontend security questions check whether you know the main attack classes precisely (what each one needs and what it can do), which defence addresses which attack, and the misconceptions: CORS is not CSRF protection, `HttpOnly` does not make XSS harmless, frameworks do not escape everything. Senior candidates should discuss defence in depth (escaping, sanitising, CSP, Trusted Types, cookie attributes), rollout strategy (report-only first), and supply-chain controls.

## Question 1: "How does React protect against XSS, and where can XSS still happen?"

**Model answer:**

> React escapes values rendered as text, so user content inserted with JSX becomes text nodes, not markup. XSS still happens through explicit escape hatches and the edges: dangerouslySetInnerHTML with unsanitised content, user-controlled URLs in href or src, such as javascript: URLs, direct DOM writes through refs, server-side templates and state serialised into script tags without escaping, third-party widgets using innerHTML, and rendering LLM or Markdown output as HTML. I sanitise any HTML with DOMPurify, validate URL schemes, and add a strict nonce-based CSP and ideally Trusted Types as defence in depth.

## Question 2: "What is a strict CSP and how would you roll one out?"

**Model answer:** Instead of allow-listing hosts, which is usually bypassable, a strict CSP uses a per-request nonce (or hashes for static pages) with `'strict-dynamic'`: only scripts carrying the nonce, and scripts they load, may run. Add `object-src 'none'` and `base-uri 'none'`, and `frame-ancestors` for clickjacking. Rollout: deploy as `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` with a reporting endpoint, remove inline handlers and `javascript:` URLs from our code, handle third-party tags, watch reports until they are clean, then enforce. Next, consider `require-trusted-types-for 'script'`, also report-only first.

## Question 3: "Explain CSRF and how you prevent it in a modern app."

**Model answer:** CSRF makes a victim's browser send an authenticated request to our site from another site, relying on cookies being attached automatically. Defences in layers: session cookies with `SameSite=Lax` or `Strict`, set explicitly; never change state on GET; reject state-changing requests whose `Sec-Fetch-Site` is cross-site or whose `Origin` is not ours; and synchroniser or signed double-submit tokens for cookie-authenticated forms, especially where same-site attackers (subdomains) are possible. Bearer-token APIs are not exposed to classic CSRF, but their tokens are exposed to XSS if stored in JavaScript-readable storage.

## Question 4: "Does CORS protect my API?"

**Model answer:** No. CORS is a browser mechanism for relaxing the same-origin policy so that pages from allowed origins can read responses. It does not stop requests from being sent: simple cross-site requests reach the server and are processed, and non-browser clients ignore CORS entirely. My API still needs authentication, authorisation and CSRF protection. CORS mistakes can create vulnerabilities, though: reflecting any origin with credentials, allowing `null`, or loose suffix matching lets other sites read authenticated data.

## Question 5: "Where should a SPA store auth tokens?"

**Model answer:** Prefer an `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite` cookie with the `__Host-` prefix, often via a backend-for-frontend that holds the real tokens, plus CSRF defences. `localStorage` makes any XSS a token-theft incident with long-lived impact. In-memory tokens with a refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie are a middle ground. None of these makes XSS harmless, because injected script can act as the user while the page is open, so XSS prevention stays the priority.

## Question 6: "How do you protect a frontend from supply-chain attacks?"

**Model answer, structured:**

1. **Install:** lockfile committed, `npm ci` in CI, install scripts disabled except allow-listed packages, scanning for known-malicious and vulnerable versions.
2. **Update:** automated PRs with a minimum release age so brand-new versions are not adopted instantly; human review of new dependencies.
3. **Publish:** trusted publishing and provenance for our packages, no long-lived npm tokens, least-privilege CI secrets.
4. **Runtime:** self-host or SRI-pin third-party scripts, strict CSP including `connect-src` to limit exfiltration, sandboxed iframes for untrusted widgets, an owned inventory of tag-manager tags.
5. **Respond:** know how to find which builds included a bad version and rotate secrets quickly.

## Quick-fire follow-ups

| Follow-up | Strong short answer |
|---|---|
| "Stored vs reflected vs DOM XSS?" | Payload in the database, in the request echoed back, or moved by client code from a source to a sink |
| "Does HttpOnly stop XSS?" | No; it stops cookie theft, not requests made by injected script |
| "SameSite Lax vs Strict?" | Lax sends cookies on cross-site top-level GET navigations; Strict never cross-site |
| "Why `Vary: Origin`?" | Dynamic CORS headers must not be cached and served to other origins |
| "Clickjacking defence?" | `frame-ancestors` in CSP, `X-Frame-Options` for legacy browsers |
| "What does `'strict-dynamic'` do?" | Trust propagates from nonce-approved scripts to scripts they load |
| "When is SRI not possible?" | When the third party serves changing or per-browser content |

## Common mistakes

- Claiming CORS prevents CSRF or protects the server.
- Believing React makes XSS impossible.
- Host allow-list CSPs with `'unsafe-inline'` that block nothing meaningful.
- Storing long-lived tokens in `localStorage` without considering XSS impact.
- Changing state on GET requests, which defeats `SameSite=Lax`.
- Loading third-party scripts from external CDNs without SRI or an inventory.

diagrams.title: Where supply-chain controls apply
diagrams.code:
flowchart TD
  Dev["Developer or CI runs install"] --> Lock{"Lockfile and npm ci?"}
  Lock -->|"no"| New["Pulls newest version, possibly malicious"]
  Lock -->|"yes"| Pinned["Installs reviewed versions"]
  Pinned --> Scripts{"Install scripts allowed?"}
  Scripts -->|"all"| Exec["Postinstall malware steals tokens"]
  Scripts -->|"allow-list only"| Build["Build"]
  Build --> Ship["Bundle shipped to users"]
  Ship --> Runtime["Third-party scripts at runtime"]
  Runtime --> SRI{"Self-hosted or SRI pinned, strict CSP?"}
  SRI -->|"no"| CDN["CDN or domain compromise reaches every user"]
  SRI -->|"yes"| Contained["Changed file refused, exfiltration limited"]

keyPoints: XSS runs attacker code in your origin; it flows from sources (URL, messages, user content) to sinks (innerHTML, eval, javascript: URLs).
Frameworks escape text bindings, but dangerouslySetInnerHTML, user URLs, ref DOM writes, serialised state and third-party widgets remain XSS paths.
A strict CSP uses per-request nonces or hashes with strict-dynamic, object-src none and base-uri none; roll out in report-only mode first.
Trusted Types make HTML sinks reject plain strings, so only audited policies (for example DOMPurify-based) can produce HTML.
CSRF relies on automatic cookies: set SameSite explicitly, never change state on GET, check Sec-Fetch-Site and Origin, and use tokens for cookie-authenticated forms.
CORS relaxes the same-origin policy for reads and is enforced by browsers only; it does not protect your server and misconfigurations leak data.
Clickjacking is stopped with CSP frame-ancestors; supply-chain risk needs lockfiles, restricted install scripts, release-age delays, SRI or self-hosting, and trusted publishing.

check.q: A React app renders <a href={profile.website}>. A user sets their website to javascript:fetch('/api/export').then(...). What is the correct fix?
options: Nothing; React escapes all attribute values so this cannot run
Validate the URL and only allow http: and https: schemes before rendering it
Wrap the link in dangerouslySetInnerHTML
Add rel="noopener" to the link
check.why: Escaping prevents markup injection, but a javascript: URL in href executes on click. Parsing with new URL() and allowing only http and https blocks the scheme; noopener addresses a different issue.

check.q: Which statement about CORS is correct?
options: CORS prevents other websites from sending POST requests to your API
Setting Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * with credentials is a safe default
CORS only matters for non-browser clients like curl
CORS lets a server allow specific origins to read its responses in browsers; it does not stop simple cross-site requests from being sent
check.why: CORS is a browser-enforced relaxation of the same-origin policy for reading responses. Simple requests still reach the server, so CSRF protection and auth are still required; * cannot be combined with credentials.

check.q: What does 'strict-dynamic' add to a nonce-based Content Security Policy?
options: Scripts loaded by an already trusted (nonce-carrying) script are also allowed, so bundler chunks need no host allow-list
It allows all inline scripts
It disables CSP in development
It blocks all third-party scripts regardless of how they are loaded
check.why: With strict-dynamic, trust propagates from nonce-approved scripts to the scripts they create, while injected scripts without the nonce stay blocked. Host lists are ignored by supporting browsers.
